notes.meaning: God told Isaiah to take a large tablet or scroll and write a short phrase on it in plain, readable letters. The phrase was Maher-shalal-hash-baz, which means hurry to the plunder. This message warned that Assyria would soon rush in to loot and defeat the enemies of Judah.

God appointed two prominent leaders, Uriah the priest and Zechariah, to act as official witnesses. They watched Isaiah record the message so everyone would know the prophecy existed before the invasion happened. This prevented skeptics from claiming the prophet wrote the prediction after the events took place.

Isaiah's wife gave birth to a son, and the Lord instructed the prophet to give the baby that same prophetic name. Every time neighbors spoke the child's name, it served as a living reminder of coming judgment. The newborn boy stood as an outward pledge that God's warning would soon come to pass.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some early church writers interpreted the prophetess as a figure of the Virgin Mary, though many Catholic commentators view her as Isaiah's wife.

notes.meaning: Before this infant was old enough to call out for his mother and father, the Assyrian army would strike. The wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria would be carried off within a couple of years. This gave the people a very short timeline for the first part of the prophecy to take place.

God warned that the people had rejected the peaceful, gently flowing waters of Shiloah in Jerusalem. This quiet stream stood for God's gentle care and the humble kingdom of David. Instead of trusting the Lord, the people placed their hopes in foreign kings and military strength.

Because the people despised God's quiet stream, the Lord promised to bring a destructive flood upon them. This raging river represented the king of Assyria and his vast, violent army. Like the Euphrates overflowing its banks during spring rains, the invaders would overwhelm the entire region.

The Assyrian army would sweep into Judah and rise like a flood right up to the nation's neck. Jerusalem would stand just above water like a head, coming dangerously close to drowning. Yet Isaiah calls the country Immanuel's land, showing that the coming Messiah guarantees His people will never be wiped out entirely.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the address to Immanuel here as an ironic warning of judgment, and they suggest Immanuel and Isaiah's newborn son may refer to the same child.

notes.meaning: Isaiah challenges all foreign nations to join forces and prepare for battle, but warns that they will be shattered. No matter how clever their war plans or how strong their troops, their schemes will collapse. Human plots cannot succeed against God's people because God is with us, which is what the name Immanuel means.

The Lord laid His hand upon Isaiah with overwhelming power to guide his prophetic work. God strictly instructed him not to follow the popular mindset or walk in the ways of the fearful crowd. Faithful leaders must let God direct them instead of drifting along with the culture.

Believers are told not to join in the public panic or call every threat a dark conspiracy. The crowd was paralyzed with terror over foreign alliances and political changes. God's people must not allow worldly fears to control their thoughts or push them into bad compromises.

The Lord of Hosts is the only One people should treat as completely holy and worthy of deep reverence. Honoring God's supreme authority drives out the paralyzing fear of human power. When we grasp how great the Lord is, our enemies appear small and powerless in comparison.

To those who trust Him, God is a safe sanctuary, like a holy refuge where they find peace. But to rebels in both Israel and Judah, He becomes an obstacle in the road that causes them to trip and a hidden snare that snaps shut. Those who reject God's ways stumble over His truth and fall into ruin.

differ.view: God ordained this stumbling so that He would protect His chosen elect while leaving hardened unbelievers to their appointed fall.
The statement that many would fall means the rejection was not total, and people stumbled because of their own choice to reject the Messiah.

notes.meaning: Isaiah was told to tie up and seal God's revealed message among his faithful disciples. Since the nation as a whole refused to listen, the truth had to be carefully protected in the hearts of those who believed. It was guarded like a sealed royal document until the day of its fulfillment arrived.

Even though God was hiding His face from the house of Jacob in discipline, Isaiah resolved to wait for Him. The prophet put his ongoing trust and hope in the Lord's promises during a very dark chapter in history. When God seems quiet, believers are called to wait patiently for His mercy to shine again.

Isaiah and the children God had given him served as living signs and symbols to the nation. Their prophetic names pointed directly to coming judgment and to the survival of a faithful remnant. The surrounding world viewed this small family as strange and foolish, yet they belonged to the Lord reigning from Mount Zion.

During national crises, unfaithful people often urge others to consult fortune-tellers and mediums who whisper and mutter mysterious sounds. Isaiah points out the absurdity of living men seeking help from the dead instead of the living God. Believers must run to the Lord who gives life rather than turning to deceptive occult practices.

The Lord directs everyone back to the written Scriptures as the only true guide for faith and life. Any voice or teaching that does not match God's revealed word contains no spiritual light at all. Those who abandon Scripture will find only confusion and have no bright morning to look forward to.

Those who walk away from God's truth will wander through the land starving, exhausted, and desperate. In their angry hunger, they will look upward and curse both their king and their God for their troubles. Wherever they turn, looking up to the sky or down to the earth, they will encounter only distress, gloom, and deep darkness.
